stem: Find the area bounded by the curve \(y^{2} = 4ax\), \(x\)-axis and the lines \(x = 0,x = a\)
solution:
**Convention used.** The X-axis is named as one of the boundaries of the region, so the region is the part of the parabola's interior lying ABOVE the X-axis (the upper branch \(y=+2\sqrt{ax}\)), between \(x=0\) and \(x=a\). This is the bank's treatment of \(y^{2}=4x\), \(x=1\), \(x=4\), \(y\geq 0\). (If instead both branches were intended, the region is symmetric about the X-axis and the area is twice the value below.)

For \(y^{2}=4ax\) with \(a>0\), the upper branch is \(y=2\sqrt{a}\,\sqrt{x}\).

\(A=\displaystyle\int_{0}^{a}y\,dx=\displaystyle\int_{0}^{a}2\sqrt{a}\,\sqrt{x}\,dx=2\sqrt{a}\displaystyle\int_{0}^{a}x^{1/2}\,dx\)

\(=2\sqrt{a}\left[\dfrac{2}{3}x^{3/2}\right]_{0}^{a}=\dfrac{4\sqrt{a}}{3}\left(a^{3/2}-0\right)=\dfrac{4}{3}\sqrt{a}\cdot a\sqrt{a}\)

\(\therefore\ A=\dfrac{4a^{2}}{3}\) sq. units.

Check by dimensions and by a special case: taking \(a=4\) gives the parabola \(y^{2}=16x\) between \(x=0\) and \(x=4\), whose upper half has area \(\int_{0}^{4}4\sqrt{x}\,dx=\dfrac{64}{3}\); the formula gives \(\dfrac{4(16)}{3}=\dfrac{64}{3}\) - the same value.

stem: Find the area of the ellipse \(\frac{x^{2}}{1} + \frac{y^{2}}{4} = 1\).
solution:
For \(\dfrac{x^{2}}{1}+\dfrac{y^{2}}{4}=1\), comparing with \(\dfrac{x^{2}}{a^{2}}+\dfrac{y^{2}}{b^{2}}=1\) gives \(a^{2}=1\), \(b^{2}=4\), i.e. \(a=1\), \(b=2\).

In the first quadrant, \(\dfrac{y^{2}}{4}=1-x^{2}\), so \(y=2\sqrt{1-x^{2}}\).

The ellipse is symmetric about both axes, so the required area is \(4\) times the first-quadrant area:

\(A=4\displaystyle\int_{0}^{1}y\,dx=4\displaystyle\int_{0}^{1}2\sqrt{1-x^{2}}\,dx=8\displaystyle\int_{0}^{1}\sqrt{1-x^{2}}\,dx\)

Using \(\displaystyle\int\sqrt{a^{2}-x^{2}}\,dx=\dfrac{x}{2}\sqrt{a^{2}-x^{2}}+\dfrac{a^{2}}{2}\sin^{-1}\dfrac{x}{a}\) with \(a=1\):

\(A=8\left[\dfrac{x}{2}\sqrt{1-x^{2}}+\dfrac{1}{2}\sin^{-1}x\right]_{0}^{1}=8\left[\left(0+\dfrac{1}{2}\cdot\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)-\left(0+0\right)\right]=8\cdot\dfrac{\pi}{4}\)

\(\therefore\ A=2\pi\) sq. units.

Check against the general formula: the area of \(\dfrac{x^{2}}{a^{2}}+\dfrac{y^{2}}{b^{2}}=1\) is \(\pi ab\), which here gives \(\pi(1)(2)=2\pi\) - the same value.

stem: Find the area of the region bounded by the curve \(y = x^{2}\), and the lines \(x = 1,x = 2\) and \(y = 0\).
solution:
The line \(y=0\) is the X-axis, and \(y=x^{2}\geq 0\) throughout \([1,2]\), so the region lies wholly above the X-axis and

\(A=\displaystyle\int_{1}^{2}y\,dx=\displaystyle\int_{1}^{2}x^{2}\,dx\)

\(=\left[\dfrac{x^{3}}{3}\right]_{1}^{2}=\dfrac{8}{3}-\dfrac{1}{3}=\dfrac{7}{3}\)

\(\therefore\ A=\dfrac{7}{3}\) sq. units.

Check: the region lies between the horizontal lines \(y=1\) and \(y=4\) over an interval of width \(1\), so its area must lie between \(1\) and \(4\); \(\dfrac{7}{3}\approx 2.33\) is consistent.

stem: Find the area of the region lying between the parabolas \(y^{2} = 4ax\) and \(x^{2} = 4ay\).
solution:
The equations of the parabolas are

\(y^{2}=4ax\)   ... (I)   and   \(x^{2}=4ay\)   ... (II)

**Points of intersection.** From (II), \(y=\dfrac{x^{2}}{4a}\). Substituting in (I):

\(\left(\dfrac{x^{2}}{4a}\right)^{2}=4ax\), i.e. \(\dfrac{x^{4}}{16a^{2}}=4ax\), so \(x^{4}=64a^{3}x\)

\(x\left(x^{3}-64a^{3}\right)=0\), i.e. \(x\left[x^{3}-(4a)^{3}\right]=0\)

\(\therefore\ x=0\) or \(x=4a\), giving the points \(O(0,0)\) and \(P(4a,4a)\).

**The area.** On \([0,4a]\) the parabola \(y^{2}=4ax\) (i.e. \(y=\sqrt{4ax}\)) lies above \(x^{2}=4ay\) (i.e. \(y=\dfrac{x^{2}}{4a}\)), so

\(A=\displaystyle\int_{0}^{4a}\sqrt{4ax}\,dx-\displaystyle\int_{0}^{4a}\dfrac{x^{2}}{4a}\,dx\)

\(=2\sqrt{a}\left[\dfrac{2}{3}x^{3/2}\right]_{0}^{4a}-\dfrac{1}{4a}\left[\dfrac{x^{3}}{3}\right]_{0}^{4a}\)

\(=\dfrac{4\sqrt{a}}{3}\left(4a\right)^{3/2}-\dfrac{1}{12a}\left(64a^{3}\right)=\dfrac{4\sqrt{a}}{3}\cdot 8a\sqrt{a}-\dfrac{16a^{2}}{3}\)

\(=\dfrac{32a^{2}}{3}-\dfrac{16a^{2}}{3}\)

\(\therefore\ A=\dfrac{16a^{2}}{3}\) sq. units.

Check: the two parabolas are reflections of each other in the line \(y=x\), so the region is symmetric about that line, and the area under \(y=\sqrt{4ax}\) must be exactly twice the area under \(y=\dfrac{x^{2}}{4a}\) over \([0,4a]\). It is: \(\dfrac{32a^{2}}{3}=2\times\dfrac{16a^{2}}{3}\).

stem: Find the area of the region bounded by the curve \(y^{2} = 4x\), the X-axis and the lines \(x = 1,x = 4\) for \(y \geq 0\).
solution:
Since \(y\geq 0\) is stated, only the upper branch of the parabola is taken: \(y^{2}=4x\) gives \(y=2\sqrt{x}\).

\(A=\displaystyle\int_{1}^{4}y\,dx=\displaystyle\int_{1}^{4}2\sqrt{x}\,dx=2\displaystyle\int_{1}^{4}x^{1/2}\,dx\)

\(=2\left[\dfrac{2}{3}x^{3/2}\right]_{1}^{4}=\dfrac{4}{3}\left[4^{3/2}-1^{3/2}\right]=\dfrac{4}{3}\left(8-1\right)\)

\(\therefore\ A=\dfrac{28}{3}\) sq. units.

Check: on \([1,4]\) the height \(2\sqrt{x}\) runs from \(2\) to \(4\), so over a width of \(3\) the area must lie between \(6\) and \(12\); \(\dfrac{28}{3}\approx 9.33\) is consistent.

stem: Find the area of the region bounded by the curve \(y = x^{2}\) and the line \(y = 4\).
solution:
The parabola \(y=x^{2}\) meets \(y=4\) where \(x^{2}=4\), i.e. at \(x=\pm 2\); the points are \((-2,4)\) and \((2,4)\).

The region is symmetric about the Y-axis, so the required area is twice the part in the first quadrant. Integrating with respect to \(y\), with \(x=\sqrt{y}\) and \(y\) running from \(0\) to \(4\):

\(A=2\displaystyle\int_{0}^{4}x\,dy=2\displaystyle\int_{0}^{4}\sqrt{y}\,dy=2\left[\dfrac{2}{3}y^{3/2}\right]_{0}^{4}=\dfrac{4}{3}\left(4^{3/2}\right)=\dfrac{4}{3}\left(8\right)\)

\(\therefore\ A=\dfrac{32}{3}\) sq. units.

Check by integrating with respect to \(x\) instead: \(A=\displaystyle\int_{-2}^{2}\left(4-x^{2}\right)dx=\left[4x-\dfrac{x^{3}}{3}\right]_{-2}^{2}=\left(8-\dfrac{8}{3}\right)-\left(-8+\dfrac{8}{3}\right)=16-\dfrac{16}{3}=\dfrac{32}{3}\) - the same value.

stem: The area bounded by the line \(y = x\), X-axis and the lines \(x = - 1\) and \(x = 4\) is equal to _________ (in square units).
solution:
**(C)** \(\dfrac{17}{2}\)

The line \(y=x\) crosses the X-axis at \(x=0\), which lies inside \([-1,4]\), so the region falls into two parts and each must be taken positively.

Below the X-axis, for \(-1\leq x\leq 0\):

\(A_{1}=\displaystyle\int_{-1}^{0}y\,dx=\displaystyle\int_{-1}^{0}x\,dx=\left[\dfrac{x^{2}}{2}\right]_{-1}^{0}=0-\dfrac{1}{2}=-\dfrac{1}{2}\)

Area is always positive, so \(A_{1}=\left|-\dfrac{1}{2}\right|=\dfrac{1}{2}\) sq. units.

Above the X-axis, for \(0\leq x\leq 4\):

\(A_{2}=\displaystyle\int_{0}^{4}x\,dx=\left[\dfrac{x^{2}}{2}\right]_{0}^{4}=\dfrac{16}{2}=8\) sq. units.

\(\therefore\ A=A_{1}+A_{2}=\dfrac{1}{2}+8=\dfrac{17}{2}\) sq. units, which is option (C).

Check geometrically: the two parts are right-angled triangles with legs \(1,1\) and \(4,4\), of areas \(\dfrac{1}{2}\) and \(8\) - total \(\dfrac{17}{2}\). (Note that \(\displaystyle\int_{-1}^{4}x\,dx=\dfrac{15}{2}\) is NOT the area, because that treats the part below the axis as negative; \(\dfrac{15}{2}\) is not offered as an option.)

stem: Find the area of the region bounded by the parabola \(y^{2} = 16x\) and its latus rectum.
solution:
For the parabola \(y^{2}=16x\), comparing with \(y^{2}=4ax\) gives \(4a=16\), so \(a=4\).

The latus rectum is the line \(x=a\), i.e. \(x=4\).

In the first quadrant \(y=4\sqrt{x}\). The region enclosed by the parabola and its latus rectum is symmetric about the X-axis (the parabola's axis), so the required area is twice the part above the X-axis:

\(A=2\displaystyle\int_{0}^{4}y\,dx=2\displaystyle\int_{0}^{4}4\sqrt{x}\,dx=8\displaystyle\int_{0}^{4}x^{1/2}\,dx\)

\(=8\left[\dfrac{2}{3}x^{3/2}\right]_{0}^{4}=\dfrac{16}{3}\left(4^{3/2}\right)=\dfrac{16}{3}\left(8\right)\)

\(\therefore\ A=\dfrac{128}{3}\) sq. units.

Check: the region is inscribed in the rectangle \(0\leq x\leq 4\), \(-8\leq y\leq 8\) of area \(64\), and a parabolic segment fills two-thirds of its circumscribing rectangle: \(\dfrac{2}{3}\times 64=\dfrac{128}{3}\) - the same value.
